title: 3-Read Friday #39: Lesson Starts, Teacher Rehearsal, and Area Misconceptions
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #39 covers lesson-start routines, coaching for teacher decision-making, and a maths misconception. Pete Foster tackles the recurring problem of inconsistent lesson starts, addressing lateness and behaviour with concrete solutions Barton says he sees needed 'in many of the schools I visit each week.' Paul Cline extends Barton's 'recent conversion' to the value of rehearsal in coaching by proposing a framework for rehearsing teacher thinking, not just visible technique -- including what Barton calls a 'brilliant' circulation diagram. Dan Draper shares a sequenced set of questions for confronting the 'area's just times' misconception in maths. Barton frames the first two as speaking directly to his own coaching practice.
points: Barton connects Foster's lesson-start post to a problem he sees firsthand 'in many of the schools I visit each week,' praising its treatment of lateness and behaviour.

He calls himself 'a recent convert to the importance and power of rehearsal when coaching,' and credits Cline's framework -- plus its 'brilliant' circulation diagram -- with pushing that thinking further into rehearsing decision-making itself.
He singles out Draper's sequenced question set on the 'area's just times' misconception as the kind of granular, subject-specific post he says he loves.
quotes: Another good one from Pete here, addressing a problem common to many of the schools I visit each week: How do you get a consistent good start to lessons?
Issues of lateness and behaviour are addressed, and potential solutions are suggested.
As regular readers will know, I am a recent convert to the importance and power of rehearsal when coaching.
Paul takes this to a new level here, suggesting a framework teachers can use to rehearse their thinking and not just their teacher 'moves'.
Dan delves deep into a way to tackle a misconception students often hold about area - that you just multiply the given lengths.
